direct: Palo Alto Networks says Fragnesia (CVE-2026-46300), a Linux kernel privilege-escalation flaw, was exploited against PAN-OS management interfaces exposed to the internet, after attackers first exploited PHP2Shell; fixed PAN-OS builds are listed in PAN-SA-2026-0015.
downstream: PHP2Shell was already used to root and in some cases wipe unpatched Check Point gateways from Oct 30, so the same entry point now reaches two firewall vendors (stated by each vendor).
A firewall rooted through its management interface can expose VPN credentials, configuration and traffic policy for the whole network (our inference from how the product works).
Any other appliance that bundles PHP with the PHP2Shell or phpAfterShell flaws may be reachable the same way (inference; no other vendor has said so).
watch_for: A CISA KEV entry for CVE-2026-46300
Other appliance vendors naming PHP2Shell or phpAfterShell in their products
Unexpected admin sessions or files on PAN-OS management interfaces
Victim reports or counts from Palo Alto Networks
who_should_care: Palo Alto Networks customers with management interfaces reachable from the internet

direct: GreyNoise says GT13 used 99 IP addresses against Check Point Security Management Servers from Oct 17 to Nov 2, reaching at least 22 organisations, running over 100 management tasks and taking data from 24 servers; it lists CVE-2026-16232 among the flaws.
downstream: A management server holds policy, credentials and configuration for every gateway it manages, so a compromise there can change or expose firewall rules across the estate (our inference from how the product works).
Victims that have not checked management-server logs since October may not know they were reached.
watch_for: A Check Point advisory or CISA KEV entry for CVE-2026-16232
Unexpected management tasks or admin sessions in SmartConsole audit logs since Oct 17
Policy pushes nobody scheduled
Further GT13 reporting or attribution

direct: An unauthenticated attacker can bypass authentication on VMware vCenter Server (CVE-2026-123890, CVSS 9.8); Google says ARMORY CASTLE exploited it as a zero-day, and Rapid7 reports activity from as early as September. Fixes include vCenter 8.0 U3m; there is no workaround.
downstream: vCenter controls every virtual machine it manages, so one compromised server can expose a whole virtual estate.
Exploitation predates the fix, so patching does not show whether a server was already entered; logs back to September matter.
watch_for: vCenter servers reachable from untrusted networks
Unexpected vCenter sign-ins or new local accounts
Hunting guidance and indicators from Google and Broadcom
Victims named in follow-up reporting

direct: Microsoft says a flaw in the Entra Connect Health API gave unauthorized read-only access to tenant-level metadata, exposed from 23 July; a fix was deployed on Nov 19 and impacted customers were told via Azure Service Health. Exposed items include tenant IDs, organisation and domain names and technical contacts' email addresses; Microsoft says no passwords, hashes, tokens or keys were exposed.
downstream: Tenant IDs, domains and named technical contacts are what a targeted phishing or help-desk vishing campaign needs, so affected tenants should expect better-aimed lures (our inference; no misuse reported).
Microsoft has not said how many organisations were affected, so customers must check Service Health themselves.
watch_for: Azure Service Health notices for your tenant
Phishing or calls naming your Entra technical contacts
A count of affected organisations from Microsoft

direct: PLAID suspended all KARTE services after a vulnerability was exploited on Nov 13; its own account emails and contacts were taken, and customer data of several hundred companies was affected in each data category. It plans a phased restart in mid-January 2027.
downstream: Customers report the scale: DHC about 19.11 million records, ZOZO about 15.18 million ZOZOTOWN customers, SMBC up to about 14 million, Marui about 8.83 million, MUFG Bank about 6.5 million, plus Sharp, Mitsumo, Timee, Mainichi Shimbun, Schoo and PLUS.

Leaked profiles (names, emails, dates of birth, purchase attributes, and for some Marui card members income) make convincing phishing in Japanese; integration credentials held by the service may open customers' own systems.
Companies that ended their KARTE contract are included, so former customers should check too.
watch_for: Further KARTE customers announcing leaks
Phishing that uses shop names, member IDs and dates of birth
Use of integration keys connected to KARTE
Regulator action by Japan's Personal Information Protection Commission

direct: Hex says an attacker exploited CVE-2026-129514 on Nov 23 to run commands on hex.pm web servers. It found no changed packages or lasting access, but cannot rule out that email addresses, password hashes, API key hashes and 2FA secrets were read; it rotated credentials.
downstream: Hex tells users to change passwords and reset 2FA; any reused password or unrotated API key is at risk (stated advice).
Elixir and Erlang teams that publish packages could see attempts to take over publisher accounts and push malicious versions (our inference; none reported).
watch_for: New package versions published by unexpected accounts
Hex follow-up findings on package integrity
Phishing aimed at Hex package maintainers

direct: The New York Times, relayed by Reuters and others, reports that the CIA and ODNI found an intrusion into a network used to gather intelligence from public sources, exposing some unclassified information; ODNI says classified systems and critical capabilities were not affected. Unnamed sources say early indicators point to China; investigators have not named who is responsible.
downstream: What analysts searched for in an open-source collection system could reveal intelligence priorities even if no classified data was touched (our inference).
Contractors and vendors that run or feed such systems may be asked to check their own access (inference; not reported).
watch_for: An official statement on scope or attribution
Advisories to contractors that support open-source intelligence platforms
Any link stated between this and the FinCEN or NCIC incidents (none so far)
who_should_care: Vendors of OSINT and analytics platforms

direct: The Justice Department filed a civil action to forfeit over $1.1 billion in USDC it says are proceeds of the Oct 29 Binance theft by North Korean cyber actors, and says it is helping Binance recover over $6 billion in stolen assets.
downstream: Stablecoin issuers and exchanges are being used as recovery points, so frozen USDC can be pursued in court (stated by the DOJ action).

The rest of the theft is being laundered through coinjoins and many wallets (Elliptic), so services that receive those funds risk freezes and legal exposure (inference from the freezing order and forfeiture).
watch_for: Further forfeiture or seizure actions
Wallet lists from Binance's ADGM freezing order reaching more services
Sanctions designations tied to the laundering

direct: NGINX Open Source and Plus from 1.9.5 with HTTP/2 can be made to run code as the nginx worker without a login; fixes are in 1.30.7 and 1.31.9, and proof-of-concept code is public for one flaw.
downstream: Xint chained one flaw with an unpatched Linux kernel SCTP bug to reach root and escape a Docker container, so a web front end can become a host compromise.

NGINX is embedded in load balancers, Kubernetes ingress controllers and appliances that update on their vendors' schedules; Synology has already listed the same CVE in DSM, so expect more appliance advisories.
watch_for: Ingress and appliance vendors shipping fixed NGINX builds
Worker crashes on HTTP/2 traffic
A Linux kernel fix and CVE for the SCTP flaw
Reports of in-the-wild exploitation
Appliance advisories naming CVE-2026-123007

direct: Genesis Lab says Douzone Bizon told it that its APO data backup server was accessed without authorisation and stored data, possibly including employees' names, resident registration numbers, account numbers and addresses, may have been taken; Incheon Airport Facilities Management names the same backup service as the cause.
downstream: Every Douzone APO backup customer may hold copies of employee and payroll data on the affected servers, so more notices are likely (our inference from the pattern of named clients).
Resident registration and bank account numbers enable identity fraud and targeted phishing against staff (inference).
watch_for: Further organisations naming Douzone Bizon's backup service
A statement from Douzone Bizon on scope and cause
PIPC investigation or guidance
who_should_care: Korean public bodies using outsourced backup
